job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Liam Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Rugby and drive to Coventry for my master's in manufacturing engineering, about half an hour each way. I'm in lectures or the workshop until three, then I help in my dad's garage, Costa Motors, for a couple of hours, mostly brakes and servicing. I did eight weeks last summer at a car parts supplier, checking brake components for flaws. I sent out about twenty applications last year, got two interviews and no offer, so I signed up for the master's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, as expected. I've never used the AI tools, because I like to see how a thing works before I trust it. At work I'd say the people shouting about it were selling something. To friends at the garage I'd say nothing changes and nobody's job is going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, that's the version I'd pick, but it doesn't solve my problem. I still haven't got a job and twenty applications came to nothing last year. The market is tight whether or not AI is any good. It's about timing, not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep helping my dad at the garage and send applications in spring, about thirty this time. I'd ask Mr Hartley, my old supervisor at the supplier, for a reference. I wouldn't change how I work, because the approach I use is fine and I don't need a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not about the technology, just about getting a first job. I'm twenty-four, I owe about sixteen thousand, and my girlfriend Hannah, who's a primary teacher, is already earning more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the AI tools. Would that count against you when applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. It would help, probably, if I knew the software the firms use. But I get slow with new programs, and I'd rather be good at drawing and quality checking than average at everything. I can see that's a risk, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say about the garage as a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad says he'd take me on at the garage if nothing else works. That's a backup, but I did four years of engineering. I don't want to waste that, and I'd feel I'd gone backwards.

say: I'd say the people shouting about AI are **selling something**.
I'd tell friends at the garage that nobody's job is **going anywhere**.
think: The market is tight whether or not **AI works**; it's about timing.
I still haven't got a **job**, and twenty applications came to nothing.
do: Finish the master's and keep helping at my dad's **garage**.
Ask Mr Hartley at the supplier for a **reference**.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, not about technology but about getting a first job.
S0.quote: I'd rather be good at drawing and quality checking than average at everything.
fieldNote: Liam's worry is **timing**, not AI; he dismisses the hype as a sales pitch.
He **avoids** new software, which he half admits could be a risk.
The garage is a **safety net** he is reluctant to use.

steps.text: Finish the manufacturing engineering master's and help at the garage
Send about thirty applications to manufacturers in spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. I'd tell my friends that new tools always come with big promises and I'll wait until they've proven themselves. If it takes over paperwork and checking, then fine, but someone still has to fix a brake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the part of my internship that was quality checking, looking at readings and writing them up, is exactly what they're describing. I think it means fewer people in that department and maybe none of the juniors. And I'm a junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stick to what I know and look for the hands-on jobs, like production and maintenance, where the machine is real. I'd perhaps take a short course on the quality software the supplier uses, because I couldn't avoid it. And I'd keep working at the garage to keep some money coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think. Not panicked. AI taking graduate jobs is like watching the weather change: you can't stop it, and I'd rather not be caught out in my work clothes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the first jobs would go to others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't have much experience, and the first jobs go to people who do. Hannah says to learn the tools anyway. I'd try one if my firm told me to, but I wouldn't start without being asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you has seen this already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Nuno, who works in an office doing orders. His boss has already said a program does half of it. He says he's relaxed, but I can see he isn't, because he's talking about learning to weld.

say: I'd say new tools always come with **big promises**, so I'll wait for proof.
I'd say someone still has to **fix a brake**.
think: The **quality checking** I did last summer is exactly what they're describing.
I'm a **junior**, and juniors go first.
do: Look for **hands-on** jobs in production and maintenance.
Take a short course on the supplier's **quality software** if I can't avoid it.
Keep working at the **garage** for income.
feel: I feel **anxious** but not panicked, like watching the weather change.
S1.quote: AI taking graduate jobs is like watching the weather change: you can't stop it, and I'd rather not be caught out in my work clothes.
fieldNote: Liam's **resistance** means he reacts rather than prepares.
He knows his internship **tasks** are the exposed ones.
His cousin Nuno's talk of **welding** shows the fear around him.

steps.text: Apply for production and maintenance roles rather than office quality jobs
Take a short course on the supplier's quality software
Keep working evenings at the family garage for income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast to say anything sensible. I'd probably keep quiet at work and see what the government says. I'd tell friends we should all keep our heads down, keep our jobs if we have them and not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth is I don't think I'd have a career. Everything I studied would be paper in two years, and I haven't even got a first job. The hands-on side is a few years behind, which is only a bit of comfort since I don't have hands-on experience yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go to my dad's garage full time, since cars still need fixing for a while. I'd cut everything: no going out, no new phone. And I'd talk to my local MP at the surgery, since my dad says that's what you do. It's not much of a plan, I'll admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be unable to think straight a lot of the time. Finishing my degree in 2028 would feel like finishing a race when they've already closed the finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans with Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sixteen thousand of loans on a degree that's useless. My parents would help, but they've got the garage to keep afloat and Dad's sixty-one. Hannah and I were going to look at flats next year, and I'd have to tell her it's off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be ashamed, and I'd hide it for a while. I'd say I'm waiting on offers when really I'd be changing oil. I'd tell her eventually, though, because she'd find out.

say: I'd say it's too fast to say anything **sensible**.
I'd tell friends to **keep their heads down** and not panic.
think: I don't think I'd have a **career**, because my degree would be paper in two years.
The hands-on side is a few years behind, but I have **no experience** yet.
do: Work **full time** at my dad's garage.
Cut **everything**: no going out and no new phone.
Talk to my local **MP** at the surgery.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, like finishing a race after the line has closed.
S2.quote: Finishing my degree in 2028 would feel like finishing a race when they've already closed the finish line.
fieldNote: Liam has **no plan** beyond the garage and admits it.
He expects to put off **telling** his girlfriend, Hannah, out of shame.
His **resistance** leaves him reaching for old, familiar fixes.

steps.text: Leave the job hunt and work full time at the family garage
Stop going out and put off buying a new phone
Visit the local MP's surgery to ask about graduate support
Tell Hannah the flat plans are off for now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to see what's real. I'd tell friends to learn a trade skill alongside the degree. At work I'd say we should be sensible and not be the first or the last to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get a job in the next year or two, then maybe four years of work before the machines catch up. It's not what I'd planned but it's a living. If I put money away, it should cover the time between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the master's, I'd take the first hands-on engineering job, probably maintenance or production. I'd put a third of my pay into savings, and I'd learn welding and the electrics side at weekends in the garage. I'd stay with the tools I already know until my firm moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a bit more grip. Five years isn't nothing. It gives me time to get ready, even if I'm slow to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you wait to see rather than move early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably wait. If it's coming in five years, a lot of what people say now will turn out to be wrong, and I'd rather see the first firms try it. It's a risk, but I've got to pick one of two risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What advice would you give someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. I'd tell a graduate like me to be handy, keep your hands dirty and keep a bit of money by. That's about it.

think: I'd get a job in the next **year or two**, then maybe four years before machines catch up.

feel: I feel **anxious**, with a bit more grip because five years isn't nothing.

fieldNote: Liam's answer to time is **trade skills**, not a new software stack.
He knows he **waits too long** and says so.
Savings and welding show a **practical** hedge.

steps.text: Take the first maintenance or production engineering job offered
Save a third of each pay packet
Learn welding and basic electrics at weekends in the garage
Wait for other firms to try new tools before using them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to be sensible. I'd tell friends not to panic. At work I'd say we'll cope like we always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be thirty-four, in a job I'd had for years, probably as a maintenance engineer or a team leader. The thinking part of work would change, but I'd have the experience to deal with it. I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take a production job, buy a small house with Hannah around thirty, and save. I'd learn the new tools only when my firm required them, and I'd do a short course then. I'd also help Dad make the garage ready for electric cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, I'd say. It's a long time. A few things would worry me, like whether the pension my parents have stays safe. But my own job, probably fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents to keep their money in boring places and keep the garage going as long as it makes sense. Cars will still need fixing for years. Dad's sixty-one, so he could retire before any of this matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would this change your plans with Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with Hannah. If there's ten years, we can plan for kids, a house and a pension. She'd probably be the one who finds the new thing first, and I'd come along behind.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to be **sensible**.
I'd tell friends we'll cope like we always do and not **panic**.
think: I'd be thirty-four in a job I'd had for **years**, maybe as a maintenance engineer.
I'd have the **experience** to deal with changes.
do: Buy a small **house** with Hannah around thirty.
Do a short **course** on new tools when my firm requires it.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, since ten years is a long time.
S4.quote: I'd tell my parents to keep their money in boring places and keep the garage going as long as it makes sense.
fieldNote: Liam feels **safe** with a decade, but his worry shifts to his **parents' pension**.
He lets his girlfriend **Hannah** lead on trying new things.
His pace is **slow but steady**, and he knows it.

steps.text: Take a production engineering job and keep it for several years
Save for a small house deposit with Hannah
Plan the house and children timeline with Hannah
Do a short course on new tools when my firm requires it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no job, no experience and no time to build either. What would help is a guaranteed training place, some honest warning from the government and my dad's garage still going. I'd also like firms to say how many juniors they plan to take.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I'm just slow at it, and I'd rather be sure than first. I'd say that's not the worst thing, but it's not great for a graduate in a hurry.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change. I'm just slow at it, and I'd rather be sure than first.
portrait: Liam is a **24-year-old** manufacturing engineering master's student from Rugby, studying after twenty applications gave no offer.
He owes about **sixteen thousand**, helps in his dad's garage and has a girlfriend, Hannah, who earns more than he does.
He is pragmatic and blames **timing**, not people, and has never used AI tools.
His resistance means he reacts instead of preparing, so his mood goes from **uneasy** to alarmed with two years.
With time he settles on **hands-on** work, saving and a house with Hannah.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because he'd have no job, no experience and no time.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed training place**, honest early warning and the garage still running.
